title: Infra team playbook: GPU fleet, capacity, cloud accounts, IaC, and CI/CD (2026)
author: Marissa Chen
content:
Summary
-------
This playbook consolidates Redwood Inference's recommended practices for GPU fleet capacity planning, cloud account and networking setup, Terraform/IaC module layout, CI/CD and build pipelines, and operational runbooks. It is intended for infra engineers, SREs, platform teams, and on-call responders.

Scope and audience
------------------
- Scope: global GPU fleet (hosted + dedicated), cloud account bootstrapping, VPC/networking baselines, Terraform module patterns, CI/CD for infra changes, and operational runbooks for capacity incidents.
- Audience: infra engineering, platform, SRE, security (for networking/account controls), and any team that requests reserved inference capacity.

Goals and high-level constraints
-------------------------------
- Maintain predictable capacity for customer SLAs while optimizing utilization (target utilization window 55%–70%).
- Keep a regional spare buffer: 20% reserved capacity per region for burst/maintenance windows.
- All infra changes must be managed via IaC (Terraform modules) and run through the CI/CD pipeline with automated checks.
- Network and account bootstrap must meet security baseline (least privilege, audit logging, VPC flow logs).

Ownership and contacts
----------------------
- Primary owner_team: engineering (infra/gpu-capacity squad).
- On-call and runbook owner: eng-sre (pager alias: #sre-oncall).
- Playbook author: Marissa Chen (marissa@redwood.com).
- Reviewers: Diego Alvarez (networking), Priya Nandakumar (security), Ethan Morales (runtime).

Capacity model (recommended targets)
-----------------------------------
| Region | Target GPUs (prod) | Utilization target | Spare buffer | Notes |
| us-west-2 | 200 GPUs | 60% | 40 GPUs (20%) | mix H100/A100; prefer H100 for large models |
| us-east-1 | 160 GPUs | 60% | 32 GPUs (20%) | reserve A100 80GB for high-memory workloads |
| eu-west-1 | 80 GPUs | 55% | 16 GPUs (20%) | focus on latency-sensitive routing |

Capacity policy and autoscaling
------------------------------
- Maintain a warm pool of pre-provisioned instances equal to 10% of regional prod capacity to reduce cold start latency.
- Autoscaler rules (high level):
  1. Scale up when average queue latency > 200ms for 3 consecutive 60s windows.
  2. Scale down when average GPU utilization < 45% for 10 minutes and queue latency < 100ms.
  3. Respect hard limits: do not exceed quota-based upper bound.
- Burst policy: allow cross-region bursting to a fallback region if local capacity is exhausted and latency SLA allows.

GPU types and placement guidance
-------------------------------
- Preferred types (ordered): H100-80GB, A100-80GB, A100-40GB, L4 for small TGI-like workloads.
- Placement: co-locate inference nodes with model cache stores in same AZ when possible to reduce KV cache latency.
- Cost optimization: use quantized model variants (8-bit/4-bit) for best-effort routes and keep full-precision on SLA routes.

Terraform / IaC module layout (recommended)
-------------------------------------------
Recommended repository structure (single responsibility modules):
- modules/cloud-account: organization-level IAM roles, Organization policies, SCPs, audit logging glue.
- modules/networking: VPCs, subnets, routing, Transit Gateway, VPC endpoints, NACLs, flow logs.
- modules/gpu-cluster: autoscaling groups / node pools, instance profiles, GPU drivers bootstrap scripts, kube labels/taints.
- modules/kms-and-secrets: KMS keys, key rotation policy, secrets engine bootstrap.
- modules/iac-bootstrap: remote state backend, workspaces, state locking, s3/terraform-cloud setup.
- modules/policies: OPA/constraints, security group baseline.

Example snippet (Terraform pattern):
```hcl
module "gpu_cluster" {
  source = "git::ssh://git@github.com/redwood/infrastructure-modules.git//modules/gpu-cluster?ref=v2026.06"

  region               = var.region
  cluster_name         = local.cluster_name
  gpu_instance_types   = ["nvidia-h100-80gb", "nvidia-a100-80gb"]
  desired_gpu_capacity = var.desired_gpu_capacity
  warm_pool_size       = max(1, floor(var.desired_gpu_capacity * 0.10))
}
```
Operational conventions for modules:
- All modules must expose a small set of inputs/outputs and never create cross-account resources implicitly.
- Module versions must be pinned in each consuming repo with automated upgrades via dependabot-style PRs.
- Remote state must be enabled with locking (DynamoDB or Terraform Cloud).

CI/CD and build pipelines
---------------------------
Pipeline components:
- Repo layout: infra/terraform (monorepo per environment), modules/ (shared).
- Pull request flow: plan -> policy checks -> security scan -> peer review -> apply.
- Tooling: Atlantis (for PR-triggered plans), Conftest/OPA for policies, Terratest for integration tests, TFSEC for security static checks.
- Environments: dev -> staging -> prod, with gated manual approvals for prod applies.

Pipeline best practices:
1. Every PR must include a terratest or smoke test for networking and permission changes.
2. Secrets and credentials are supplied via runner role with short-lived tokens; never checked into Git.
3. Use a separate service account for Atlantis with least privilege.
4. Run an automated drift detection job daily and alert to #infra-drift if drift > 2 resources.

Change management and approvals
------------------------------
- For changes that affect capacity/quotas or networking, require:
  - Owner sign-off from GPU-capacity squad,
  - Security review for any new ingress or IAM changes, and
  - SRE approval for runbook updates.
- Major upgrades (kernel/runtime) follow a canary rollout: canary region -> 10% -> 50% -> 100% with automated rollback on defined quality regressions.

Operational runbooks (high-level)
--------------------------------
1) Capacity exhaustion (queue depth increases, unable to serve):
  - Pager triggers to #sre-oncall.
  - Triage: check regional capacity dashboard (grafana) and autoscaler logs.
  - Immediate mitigations (in order):
    a. Expand autoscaler upper bound for region (if quota permits).
    b. Trigger emergency cross-region traffic routing to fallback region.
    c. Promote quantized model routes for non-SLA customers (rate-limit).
  - Postmortem: update capacity plan and provisioning lead time docs.

2) Node / driver failure with OOMs on GPU nodes:
  - Isolate affected nodes by cordoning in k8s and draining pods.
  - Attach kernel/GPU logs: /var/log/nvidia-installer.log, dmesg, kubelet logs.
  - If widespread, revert to previous driver AMI via launch template rollback.

3) Network outage between AZs impacting KV cache:
  - Failover read traffic to regional cache replicas.
  - If replication lag > threshold, fall back to model cold-start path and raise incident.

Incident communications and SLAs
-------------------------------
- Incidents affecting 5%+ customer traffic should be escalated to on-call manager and product ops within 30 minutes.
- SLA targets (customer-facing):
  - P99 latency: <= 800ms (text generation), <= 200ms (embeddings)
  - Availability: 99.95% monthly for Dedicated clusters
- Internal SLOs: maintain mean GPU utilization in target window (55%–70%) and no more than 1 unplanned capacity event per quarter.

Day-2 operations and checklist for provisioning a new region/cluster
-------------------------------------------------------------------
Pre-provisioning checklist:
1. Confirm account quotas and request increases (GPUs, ENIs, vCPUs).
2. Create cloud-account via modules/cloud-account and run automated smoke tests.
3. Provision VPC and subnets with modules/networking; enable flow logs and route tables.
4. Deploy gpu-cluster module to staging and run end-to-end smoke tests (inference smoke, KV cache, autoscaler behavior).
5. Validate IAM roles, KMS keys, and logging/monitoring exports.
6. Run canary traffic for 24h and verify metrics against SLA.

Checklist for decommissioning
----------------------------
- Drain cluster and verify zero running inference jobs.
- Snapshot/capture any model cache state needed for audits.
- Remove DNS entries, reduce autoscaler target to zero, and delete resources via IaC.
- Retain logs and audit trails for 90 days per retention policy.

Operational metrics and dashboards (minimum set)
------------------------------------------------
- Regional GPU capacity: requested vs available vs used.
- Queue latency distribution (p50/p90/p99).
- GPU utilization (per instance type).
- Autoscaler actions (scale up/down events).
- Kernel/driver failure rate.
- Network error rates and cross-AZ latency.

FAQ / common pitfalls
--------------------
- Q: Why keep utilization at 55%–70% instead of 80%+?
  A: Higher steady utilization increases risk of capacity exhaustion during bursts and reduces headroom for redundancy and maintenance.
- Q: When should we use on-demand vs reserved instances?
  A: Use reserved / savings plans for baseline capacity. Use on-demand for burst buffer and canary testing.

Appendix: Useful commands and snippets
-------------------------------------
- Check autoscaler logs (Kubernetes): kubectl -n infra logs deploy/autoscaler --since=1h
- Force scale (example for emergency): terraform apply -var='desired_gpu_capacity=XXX' -target=module.gpu_cluster.aws_autoscaling_group.main
- Run terratest suite: GOFLAGS='-run TestInfraSmoke' go test ./test -v
